title: All Spicy, All Vegetarian, All Curry: Three Indian Food Myths That Persist
excerpt: Three labels — spicy, vegetarian, curry — get applied to all Indian food, and all three fall apart on contact with an actual Indian kitchen.
body:
• Not all Indian food is spicy — regional cuisines like Gujarati and Kashmiri lean sweet and mild, and even within "spicy" cuisines, everyday home cooking is far gentler than restaurant fare.
  • Indian food is not uniformly vegetarian — coastal, Kashmiri, Bengali, Goan and Chettinad traditions are built around seafood, mutton and poultry.
  • "Curry" is not a single dish or spice — there is no curry powder in a traditional Indian kitchen, and the word lumps together hundreds of distinct preparations.

The shorthand that flattens a continent's food

Ask someone who has never been to India what Indian food is like and the answer arrives in seconds: spicy, vegetarian, curry. The three labels are so persistent that The Hindu has joined the long line of publications taking them apart — and each collapses the moment you look at an actual Indian kitchen.

Myth 1: It's all spicy

Heat in Indian food is regional, seasonal and personal — never a default. Gujarati thalis carry a deliberate sweetness; Kashmiri rogan josh is aromatic rather than fiery; traditional South Indian home cooking, outside Andhra Pradesh, is gentler than its restaurant reputation suggests. Chettinad matriarch Meenakshi Meyyappan has said her region's famed cuisine is made "very temperate and the taste is subtle" — with more coriander seed than chillies. The scorching stereotype comes largely from restaurant menus calibrated for diners who equate Indian with hot, not from the way families eat at home.

Myth 2: It's all vegetarian

India has the world's largest vegetarian population, but a majority of Indians eat meat. Coastal cuisines from Goa, Kerala, Mangalore and Bengal are built on fish and seafood; Kashmir is famous for mutton rogan josh and gushtaba; Chettinad cooking includes mutton and chicken kozhambu and offal soup. The vegetarian reputation reflects Hindu-majority dietary traditions in the Gangetic belt — real enough, but it erases entire regional cuisines where non-vegetarian dishes are the centerpiece.

Myth 3: It's all "curry"

No traditional Indian kitchen contains a jar labeled curry powder. "Curry" is a colonial-era catch-all that flattens hundreds of distinct preparations — kuzhambu, kootu, saalan, rassa, poriyal — each with its own spice architecture, into a single word. Masalas are ground fresh for the dish, often on a stone ammi, and vary by household. Ordering "a curry" at an Indian restaurant is a little like ordering "a soup" in France and expecting it to mean one thing.

Why the myths stick

The stereotypes persist partly because they contain a grain of truth: some Indian food is very spicy, much of it is vegetarian, and gravy-based dishes are common. They also persist because the diaspora's first ambassadors were restaurant curries and takeaway menus, which optimized for the familiar. But for anyone cooking at home — or traveling across India's 28 states and eight union territories — the reality is a cuisine defined by regional variety, not by the three words that describe it abroad. Believing the myths isn't just inaccurate; it keeps you from the food itself.
